lessons.title: Positioning a Portfolio for Currency War Risk

body.text: This course's real payoff isn't trivia about 1934 or 2015. It's a checklist you can actually run the next time a currency war headline crosses your terminal, before you touch a single position.

children.text: Every case study in this course rewarded getting the diagnosis right before deciding what to do. Four questions, asked in order, cover almost everything this course has taught.

children.text: Step 2: Map Your Actual Currency Exposure

Currency exposure in a typical Indian portfolio hides in three layers, and most investors only ever check the first. Direct exposure comes from foreign holdings: US equities via an LRS-funded account, offshore mutual funds, or ADRs. Indirect exposure comes from sector composition, an IT and pharma-heavy equity book is an implicit long-dollar, short-rupee earnings bet, while an oil marketing company or aviation-heavy book is the reverse. The third and most overlooked layer is balance sheet exposure: does a company you hold carry unhedged foreign currency borrowings that get costlier in rupee terms the moment the currency weakens? This is checkable directly in the borrowings note of a company's annual report, or the balance sheet section on screener.in.

body.title: Map Your Portfolio's Currency Exposure This Week
steps: List your portfolio's sector weights and flag which sectors carry material direct FX revenue or cost exposure (IT, pharma, oil marketing, aviation, metals)
For every foreign holding (US equity funds, ADRs, offshore ETFs), confirm whether the product is currency-hedged or unhedged
Check your largest domestic holdings' borrowings notes on screener.in or in the annual report for unhedged foreign currency debt
Estimate what percentage of your portfolio's value would move, directionally, from a hypothetical 5% adverse INR move
Confirm your current gold or hard-asset allocation against your intended strategic target

children.text: Step 3: Build Natural Hedges Before You Need Them

markDefs.definition: A portfolio holding whose value tends to move in the opposite direction of a specific risk, offsetting it without requiring an active derivatives position, such as gold during currency instability or unhedged foreign equities during a sharp domestic currency devaluation.

children.text: The cheapest hedges are structural ones built ahead of time, not reactive trades placed mid-panic. A strategic gold allocation, commonly in the 5 to 10% range via sovereign gold bonds or gold ETFs, has historically behaved as a

against currency instability, echoing the safe-haven demand covered in the last lesson. Some deliberately unhedged exposure to global assets works similarly in reverse: if the rupee suffers a genuine 1991 or 2013-style devaluation, unhedged dollar assets rise in rupee terms at exactly the moment domestic assets are under the most pressure, a natural offset rather than an active bet.

The same logic argues against a portfolio built entirely around one currency-war thesis, all-in on IT because rupee weakness helps margins, or all-in on oil marketing companies as a bet on a stable rupee. Chapter 3 showed sector effects can offset or reinforce each other unpredictably depending on the shock's actual driver. A barbell across sectors with opposite currency sensitivities survives being wrong about the direction of the next shock; a concentrated single-thesis bet does not.
Step 4: Watch the Leading Indicators, Not Just the Headlines

children.text: The single most common mistake this course has flagged repeatedly is trading the first 48 hours of a currency shock as if it were the final verdict. Rebalancing sector weights based on Day 2 risk-off selling, before any fundamental repricing has had time to occur, means reacting to sentiment rather than substance. The discipline this course argues for isn't inaction, it's sequencing: diagnose first, map exposure, confirm your structural hedges are already in place, then wait for the fundamental window before making sector-specific changes.

body.title: The Capstone: Run the Full Framework
body.scenario: You manage a ₹500 crore multi-asset fund for a family office. The equity book is 25% IT services, 10% oil marketing companies, and the remainder in domestic-consumption names, alongside a 15% allocation to US equities through an unhedged offshore fund and a 5% strategic gold allocation. The Fed looks set to begin a new rate-cutting cycle next quarter, and emerging market currencies, including the rupee, have started strengthening in anticipation.
body.prompt: Walk through this lesson's five-step framework for this exact portfolio. What do you check first, and what, if anything, would you actually change?
body.modelAnswer: Step 1, diagnose: rupee strength here is market-anticipated (a Fed cutting cycle, capital flowing toward EM ahead of the move), not a deliberate Indian policy devaluation or crisis, closer to the 2010 currency war setup than to a 1991-style shock. Step 2, map exposure: the 25% IT weight is an implicit short-dollar bet that a strengthening rupee works against on the margin side, the unhedged 15% US equity sleeve is a direct dollar exposure that a rupee appreciation would also work against in rupee terms, and the 10% OMC weight would actually benefit from rupee strength through cheaper crude. Step 3, hedges: the portfolio's structural mix already has some natural offset built in (OMC weight cushions IT weakness somewhat), but both the IT overweight and the unhedged US sleeve point the same direction here, both hurt by a strengthening rupee, which is a concentration risk worth flagging even though neither position alone looks extreme. Step 4, leading indicators: check whether this looks like the early stage of a 2010-style capital flow wave (watch reserve accumulation, since RBI buying dollars to cap the rupee would be the tell) versus a more durable structural shift. Step 5, discipline: since this is an anticipated, gradual Fed cycle rather than a sudden shock, there is no risk-off noise to wait out here, so it is reasonable to act on the diagnosis now rather than waiting. The concrete change: trim the IT overweight modestly and consider partially hedging the offshore equity sleeve, not because either position is wrong, but because both currently point the same direction on the one risk this analysis just surfaced, and the gold and OMC positions already provide some of the portfolio's diversification against the opposite scenario, a sharp rupee weakening, which the fund would otherwise be leaning away from being able to handle.

body.title: Course Recap: Lock In the Core Vocabulary

cards.definition: A deliberate central bank action to weaken a currency for trade advantage, distinct from market depreciation or a currency crisis.
A trade-weighted, inflation-adjusted measure of a currency's actual competitiveness, distinct from its nominal exchange rate.
A country can hold at most two of: a fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility, and independent monetary policy.
Currency shocks hit markets first through broad, indiscriminate risk-off selling, then through slower, sector-specific fundamental repricing.
A portfolio holding, such as gold or unhedged foreign assets, that offsets a specific risk structurally, without an active derivatives position.

points: Diagnose the mechanism first: deliberate policy, market depreciation, or crisis, using the four-question checklist before making any portfolio decision.
Map currency exposure across all three layers: direct foreign holdings, sector-level FX sensitivity, and individual companies' unhedged foreign currency debt.
Build structural hedges, a strategic gold allocation and some deliberately unhedged global exposure, before a shock hits rather than scrambling for them mid-panic.
Track REER divergence, reserve trends, rate differential crowding and central bank communication tone as leading indicators, not just headline currency levels.
Respect the two-speed market: don't mistake the first 48 hours of risk-off selling for the fundamental verdict that only shows up over the following quarter.

This closes the course. Every framework here, from the 1930s gold standard to the 2024 yen unwind, points to the same discipline: understand the mechanism, map the real exposure, and let time separate sentiment from substance before you act.
